newsitem.title: SOUTH AFRICA: S.AFRICAN ASSASSIN IMPLICATES P.W. BOTHA.
newsitem.headline: S.AFRICAN ASSASSIN IMPLICATES P.W. BOTHA.

text.p: A convicted government assassin of South Africa's apartheid era implicated former president P.W. Botha on Monday when he lifted the lid on numerous killings of anti-apartheid activists.

Eugene de Kock, who is pleading for leniency before he is sentenced, was found guilty last month of six murders and scores of lesser crimes committed while he led a notorious death squad unit hunting down guerrillas of the black liberation movement.
De Kock faces a maximum sentence of life imprisonment, which in South Africa commonly means 25 years.
But he has applied for full amnesty from the Truth and Reconciliation Commission, hinting that he is ready to name those behind crimes committed in the name of racial segregation.

"I have no doubt state president P.W. Botha knew about it," he told a hushed Pretoria Supreme Court, referring to the 1985 cross-border raid to the tiny mountain kingdom of Lesotho which is ensconced by South Africa.
African National Congress (ANC) activists Leon Meyer and Jacqueline Quinn and about eight others were killed in the raid, but their baby daughter Phoenix and a babysitter survived.

"All the military intelligence, police intelligence and national intelligence also knew, as did the commissioner of police and Brigadier (Willem) Schoon," said de Kock, who testified he had suffered years of nightmares after carrying out killings on orders from his seniors.
All those involved in the December 20, 1985 raid were rewarded with medals and certificates afterwards, he added.
De Kock, who named several high-ranking police officers and generals in Monday's hearing, said his immediate boss, Schoon, had instructed him to carry out the Lesotho operation.
Just prior to the orders, he said, Botha had accused Lesotho of allowing ANC guerrillas to use it as a base to launch attacks on South Africa.

He said Schoon, in the presence of then security branch head General Johan van der Merwe -- later appointed as national police commissioner by last white president F.W. de Klerk -- approved the necessary plans.

De Kock, 47, also detailed several attacks, abductions and murders in neighbouring Swaziland. He once claimed to be apartheid's most effective assassin but his defence lawyers say he now suffers from post-traumatic stress disorder.
The career policeman, arrested shortly after the all-race elections in 1994 buried apartheid, took a break for medication during his day's testimony.
"At one stage I was too scared to go to sleep," he told Judge Willem van der Merwe. "I would have nightmares of fights, burning grass...you feel you're awake but you can't move."
De Kock continues his testimony on Tuesday.
